description: Test your knowledge of Microcytic anemia through blood smear morphology, diagnostic features, and clinical pattern recognition.

cards.text: What is the correct sequence for reading a blood smear, and what is the key rule before drawing conclusions?
cards.answer: Start at 10× (distribution scan in monolayer), then 40× (initial morphology), finally 100× oil immersion (confirm findings). Follow the '4-field rule'—observe at least 4 oil fields before concluding.

tip.tip: 10-40-100: Low power finds the area, medium power spots abnormality, oil confirms the diagnosis

cards.text: How do you identify microcytosis on blood smear without a hemocytometer?
cards.answer: RBCs should be approximately the same diameter as the nucleus of a small lymphocyte (~7 µm). Microcytic RBCs are clearly smaller than this reference nucleus.

tip.tip: Lymphocyte nucleus = natural gold standard for size comparison

cards.text: Define hypochromia in terms of central pallor. What percentage indicates abnormality?
cards.answer: Normal RBCs have central pallor occupying ~1/3 of cell diameter. Hypochromic RBCs have central pallor >1/3; in severe IDA, cells appear as pale rings ('pessary cells').

tip.tip: The 1/3 rule: Normal = 1/3 pallor; Abnormal = >1/3 pallor

cards.text: What RBC shapes are characteristic of Iron Deficiency Anemia, and which shapes suggest other diagnoses?
cards.answer: Pencil cells (elongated microcytes) are classic for IDA. Target cells suggest thalassemia; teardrop cells indicate myelofibrosis or severe hemolysis.

tip.tip: Pencil cells = IDA; Target cells = Thal; Teardrops = myelofibrosis

cards.text: What does basophilic stippling represent, and which conditions feature it prominently?
cards.answer: Coarse dark blue dots representing precipitated ribosomes. Seen in thalassemia, lead poisoning, and sideroblastic anemia—NOT typically in simple IDA.

tip.tip: Blue dots = ribosomal RNA; signals abnormal hemoglobin synthesis or toxicity

cards.text: What are Pappenheimer bodies, how are they visualized, and what is their diagnostic significance?
cards.answer: Iron-containing granules (siderosomes) visible as faint dots on Leishman stain. Confirmed with Perl's Prussian blue stain (turn blue). Classic marker of sideroblastic anemia, NOT iron deficiency.

tip.tip: Pappenheimer = iron storage granules; indicates sideroblastic anemia, not IDA

cards.text: Name the four systematic parameters for characterizing RBC abnormalities on blood smear.
cards.answer: Size (MCV indicator via microcytosis), Colour (MCH/MCHC via hypochromia), Shape (anisopoikilocytosis and specific morphologies like pencil/target cells), Content (inclusions like basophilic stippling, Pappenheimer bodies).

tip.tip: S-C-S-C framework: Size, Color, Shape, Content—never skip any parameter

cards.text: In Iron Deficiency Anemia, which appears first on blood smear: microcytosis or hypochromia?
cards.answer: Microcytosis is the earliest morphologic feature (MCV drops before MCHC). RBCs become smaller than the lymphocyte nucleus reference before marked color loss is visible.

tip.tip: IDA begins with size reduction, then color loss follows—MCV drops first
